title: How to Patch a Small Hole in Drywall
meta: Patch nail holes, anchor holes and dents up to about 1 1/2 inches, and holes up to 6 inches with a self-adhesive mesh patch, using thin coats of compound.
summary: Fill nail holes and dents with spackling or joint compound in two or three thin coats, sanding lightly between. For holes from about 1 1/2 to 6 inches, cover the hole with a self-adhesive metal or mesh patch first, then feather three thin coats of compound over it, prime and paint.
time: 30 minutes of work, plus drying time
causes: Small holes come from nails, anchors, doorknobs and furniture. The key to an invisible patch is thin coats: compound shrinks as it dries, so one thick coat cracks and sinks. Larger holes need something to bridge the gap.

materials.name: Lightweight spackling or all-purpose joint compound
Self-adhesive wall repair patch, 4 or 6 inch
materials.q: drywall repair patch kit self adhesive

materials.name: Primer
materials.note: Keeps the patch from showing through paint

materials.name: Touch-up paint
materials.q: paint tray and mini roller kit

steps.title: Prep the hole
steps.text: Cut away torn paper and loose bits with a utility knife. Press a dent so nothing sticks out. For an anchor hole, pull or push in the anchor and trim it flush.

steps.title: Small holes: fill in thin coats
steps.text: Press compound into the hole with a small putty knife, then scrape across to leave it slightly above the surface. Let it dry fully. Apply a second thin coat a little wider. This Old House recommends two or three thin, smooth coats.

steps.title: Medium holes: apply a patch
steps.text: Center a self-adhesive patch over the hole and press it flat. It should overlap solid drywall on every side.

steps.title: Feather the compound
steps.text: With the 6 inch knife, spread a thin coat over the patch extending a couple of inches past it. Let it dry, then apply two more coats, each wider and thinner, to hide the edges.

steps.title: Sand lightly
steps.text: Sand with a fine sponge until smooth and flush. Run your hand over it; you should not feel a ridge. Wipe off dust.

steps.title: Prime and paint
steps.text: Prime the patch, then paint, feathering beyond the repair so it blends.

safety: Homes built before 1978 may have lead paint. Do not dry-sand old paint until you know; follow EPA lead-safe practices.
Before cutting or drilling into a wall, think about pipes and wires behind it. Wiring often runs vertically beside outlets and switches.
Wear a dust mask when sanding.
call_pro: The hole is from a water leak; fix the leak and check for mold first.
The wall is plaster and the plaster is crumbling or loose from the lath.
The same crack or hole area keeps coming back.

faq.a: Lightweight spackle is easy for small holes and dries fast. All-purpose joint compound is better for larger patches and feathering wide areas.

faq.q: How long does compound need to dry?
faq.a: It depends on thickness, humidity and the product; read the label. Thin coats of lightweight spackle can dry within an hour; joint compound often needs several hours to overnight.

faq.q: Why does my patch show through the paint?
faq.a: Unprimed compound absorbs paint differently from the wall. Prime the patch and paint a wider area.
